entries.fb1125bdfb542c1074f0d278814a33abd793c70a: <div sID="gen9099" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Esth.9" sID="Esth.9"/> <div eID="gen9099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9100" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9101" type="x-p"/> We left two royal edicts in force, both given at the court of Shushan, one bearing date the thirteenth day of the first month, appointing that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month then next ensuing all the Jews should be killed; another bearing date the twenty-third day of the third month, empowering the Jews, on the day appointed for their slaughter, to draw the sword in their own defence and make their part good against their enemies as well as they could. Great expectation there was, no doubt, of this day, and the issue of it. The Jews' cause was to be tried by battle and the day was fixed for the combat by authority. Their enemies resolved not to lose the advantages given them by the first edict, in hope to overpower them by numbers; the Jews relied on the goodness of their God and the justice of their cause, and resolved to make their utmost efforts against their enemies. The day comes at length; and here we are told, I. What a glorious day it was, that year, to the Jews, and the two days following—a day of victory and triumph, both in the city Shushan and in all the rest of the king's provinces, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.1-Esth.9.19">ver. 1-19</reference>. II. What a memorable day it was made to posterity, by an annual feast, in commemoration of this great deliverance, called "the feast of Purim," <reference osisRef="Esth.9.20-Esth.9.32">ver. 20-32</reference>.
entries.2e1f0023fa59b194e0c95b7094b75bf90f0753c6: <div eID="gen9101" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9100" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Jews Avenged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 509.)</title> <div sID="gen9102" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the twelfth month, that <hi type="italic">is,</hi> the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over them that hated them;) <hi type="super">2</hi> The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, to lay hand on such as sought their hurt: and no man could withstand them; for the fear of them fell upon all people. <hi type="super">3</hi> And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them. <hi type="super">4</hi> For Mordecai <hi type="italic">was</hi> great in the king's house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces: for this man Mordecai waxed greater and greater. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thus the Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and destruction, and did what they would unto those that hated them. <hi type="super">6</hi> And in Shushan the palace the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha, <hi type="super">8</hi> And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha, <hi type="super">9</hi> And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha, <hi type="super">10</hi> The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand. <hi type="super">11</hi> On that day the number of those that were slain in Shushan the palace was brought before the king. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the king said unto Esther the queen, The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in Shushan the palace, and the ten sons of Haman; what have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? now what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: or what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy request further? and it shall be done. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then said Esther, If it please the king, let it be granted to the Jews which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in Shushan to do to morrow also according unto this day's decree, and let Haman's ten sons be hanged upon the gallows. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the king commanded it so to be done: and the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman's ten sons. <hi type="super">15</hi> For the Jews that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Shushan gathered themselves together on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar, and slew three hundred men at Shushan; but on the prey they laid not their hand. <hi type="super">16</hi> But the other Jews that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the king's provinces gathered themselves together, and stood for their lives, and had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes seventy and five thousand, but they laid not their hands on the prey, <hi type="super">17</hi> On the thirteenth day of the month Adar; and on the fourteenth day of the same rested they, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. <hi type="super">18</hi> But the Jews that <hi type="italic">were</hi> at Shushan assembled together on the thirteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> thereof, and on the fourteenth thereof; and on the fifteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the same they rested, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. <hi type="super">19</hi> Therefore the Jews of the villages, that dwelt in the unwalled towns, made the fourteenth day of the month Adar <hi type="italic">a day of</hi> gladness and feasting, and a good day, and of sending portions one to another. <div eID="gen9102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9103" type="x-p"/> We have here a decisive battle fought between the Jews and their enemies, in which the Jews were victorious. Neither side was surprised; for both had notice of it long enough before, so that it was a fair trial of skill between them. Nor could either side call the other <hi type="italic">rebels,</hi> for they were both supported by the royal authority. <div eID="gen9103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9104" type="x-p"/> I. The enemies of the Jews were the aggressors. They hoped, notwithstanding the latter edict, <hi type="italic">to have power over them,</hi> by virtue of the former (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.1">v. 1</reference>), and made assaults upon them accordingly; they formed themselves into bodies, and joined in confederacy against them, to <hi type="italic">seek their hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.2">v. 2</reference>. The Chaldee paraphrase says that none appeared against the Jews but Amalekites only, who were infatuated, and had their hearts hardened, as Pharaoh's against Israel, to take up arms to their own destruction. Some had such an inveterate implacable malice against the Jews that Haman's fall and Mordecai's advancement, instead of convincing them, did but exasperate them, and make them the more outrageous and resolute to cut all their throats. The sons of Haman, particularly, vowed to avenge their father's death, and pursue his designs, which they call <hi type="italic">noble and brave,</hi> whatever hazards they run; and a strong party they had formed both in Shushan and in the provinces in order hereunto. Fight they would, though they plainly saw Providence fight against them; and thus they were infatuated to their own destruction. If they would have sat still, and attempted nothing against the people of God, not a hair of their head would have fallen to the ground: but they cannot persuade themselves to do that; they must be meddling, though it prove to their own ruin, and roll a burdensome stone, which will return upon them. <div eID="gen9104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9105" type="x-p"/> II. But the Jews were the conquerors. That very day when the king's decree for their destruction was to be put in execution, and which the enemies thought would have been <hi type="italic">their</hi> day, proved <hi type="italic">God's</hi> day, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">turned to the contrary</hi> of what was expected, and <hi type="italic">the Jews had rule over those that hated them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.1">v. 1</reference>. We are here told, <div eID="gen9105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9106" type="x-p"/> 1. What the Jews did for themselves (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">They gathered themselves together in their cities,</hi> embodied, and stood upon their defence, offering violence to none, but bidding defiance to all. If they had not had an edict to warrant them, they durst not have done it, but, being so supported, they strove lawfully. Had they acted separately, each family apart, they would have been an easy prey to their enemies; but acting in concert, and gathering together in their cities, they strengthened one another, and durst face their enemies. <hi type="italic">Vis unita fortior—forces act most powerfully when combined.</hi> Those that write of the state of the Jews at this day give this as a reason why, though they are very numerous in many parts, and very rich, they are yet so despicable, because they are generally so selfish that they cannot incorporate, and, being under the curse of dispersion, they cannot unite, nor (as here) <hi type="italic">gather together,</hi> for, if they could, they might with their numbers and wealth threaten the most potent states. <div eID="gen9106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9107" type="x-p"/> 2. What the rulers of the provinces did for them, under the influence of Mordecai. All the officers of the king, who, by the bloody edict, were ordered to help forward their destruction (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.12-Esth.3.13">ch. iii. 12, 13</reference>), conformed to the latter edict (which, being an estopel against an estopel, had set the matter at large, and left them at liberty to observe which they pleased) and <hi type="italic">helped the Jews,</hi> which turned the scale on their side, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.3">v. 3</reference>. The provinces would generally do as the rulers of the provinces inclined, and therefore their favouring the Jews would greatly further them. But why did they help them? Not because they had any kindness for them, but because <hi type="italic">the fear of Mordecai fell upon them,</hi> he having manifestly the countenance both of God and the king. They all saw it their interest to help Mordecai's friends because he was not only great in the king's house, and caressed by the courtiers (as many are who have no intrinsic worth to support their reputation), but <hi type="italic">his fame</hi> for wisdom and virtue <hi type="italic">went out</hi> thence <hi type="italic">throughout all the provinces:</hi> in all places he was extolled as a great man. He was looked upon also as a thriving man, and one that <hi type="italic">waxed greater and greater</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.4">v. 4</reference>), and therefore for fear of him all the king's officers helped the Jews. Great men may, by their influence, do a great deal of good; many that fear not God will stand in awe of them. <div eID="gen9107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9108" type="x-p"/> 3. What God did for them: he struck <hi type="italic">all people</hi> with a <hi type="italic">fear of them</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.2">(v. 2</reference>), as the Canaanites were made afraid of Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.9">Josh. ii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.5.1">v. 1</reference>), so that, though they had so much hardiness as to assault them, yet they had not courage to prosecute the assault. Their hearts failed them when they came to engage, and <hi type="italic">none of the men of might could find their hands.</hi> <div eID="gen9108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9109" type="x-p"/> 4. What execution they did hereupon: <hi type="italic">No man could withstand them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.2">v. 2</reference>), but <hi type="italic">they did what they would to those that hated them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.5">v. 5</reference>. So strangely were the Jews strengthened and animated, and their enemies weakened and dispirited, that none of those who had marked themselves for their destruction escaped, but they <hi type="italic">smote them with the stroke of the sword.</hi> Particularly, (1.) On the thirteenth day of the month Adar they slew in the city Shushan 500 men (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.6">v. 6</reference>) and the ten sons of <hi type="italic">Haman,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.10">v. 10</reference>. The Jews, when on the feast of Purim they read this book of Esther, oblige themselves to read the names of Haman's ten sons all in one breath, without any pause, because they say that they were all killed together, and all gave up the ghost just in the same moment.—<hi type="italic">Buxt. Synag. Jud.</hi> c. 24. The Chaldee paraphrase says that, when these ten were slain, Zeresh, with seventy more of his children, escaped, and afterwards begged their bread from door to door. (2.) On the fourteenth day they slew in Shushan 300 more, who had escaped the sword on the former day of execution, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.15">v. 15</reference>. This Esther obtained leave of the king for them to do, for the greater terror of their enemies, and the utter crushing of that malignant party of men. The king had taken account of the numbers that were put to the sword the first day (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.11">v. 11</reference>), and told Esther (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.12">v. 12</reference>), and asked her what more she desired. "Nothing," says she, "but commission to do such another day's work." Esther surely was none of the blood-thirsty, none of those that delight in slaughter, but she had some very good reasons that moved her to make this request. She also desired that the dead bodies of Haman's ten sons might be hanged up on the gallows on which their father was hanged, for the greater disgrace of the family and terror of the party (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.13">v. 13</reference>), and it was done accordingly, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.14">v. 14</reference>. It is supposed that they were hanged in chains and left hanging for some time. (3.) The Jews in the country kept to their orders, and slew no more of their enemies than what were slain the thirteenth day, which were in all, among all the provinces, 75,000, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.16">v. 16</reference>. If all these were Amalekites (as the Jews say), surely now it was that the remembrance of Amalek was <hi type="italic">utterly put out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exod. xvii. 14</reference>. However, that which justifies them in the execution of so many is that they did it in their own just and necessary defence; they <hi type="italic">stood for their lives,</hi> authorized to do so by the law of self-preservation, as well as by the king's decree. (4.) In these several executions it is taken notice of that on the prey they laid not their hand, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.10">v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.16">16</reference>. The king's commission had warranted them to <hi type="italic">take the spoil</hi> of their enemies <hi type="italic">for a prey</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>), and a fair opportunity they had of enriching themselves with it; if Haman's party had prevailed, no doubt, they would have made use of their authority to seize the goods and estates of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>. But the Jews would not do so by them, [1.] That they might, to the honour of their religion, evidence a holy and generous contempt of worldly wealth, in imitation of their father Abraham, who scorned to enrich himself with the spoils of Sodom. [2.] That they might make it appear that they aimed at nothing but their own preservation, and used their interest at court for the saving of their lives, not for the raising of their estates. [3.] Their commission empowered them to destroy the families of their enemies, even the <hi type="italic">little ones</hi> and <hi type="italic">the women,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>. But their humanity forbade them to do that, though that was designed against them. They slew none but those they found in arms; and therefore they did not take the spoil, but left it to the women and little ones, whom they spared, for their subsistence; otherwise as good slay them as starve them, take away their lives as take away their livelihoods. Herein they acted with a consideration and compassion well worthy of imitation. <div eID="gen9109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9110" type="x-p"/> 5. What a satisfaction they had in their deliverance. The Jews in the country cleared themselves of their enemies on the thirteenth day of the month, and they rested on the fourteenth day (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.17">v. 17</reference>), and made that a thanksgiving day, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">v. 19</reference>. The Jews in Shushan, the royal city, took two days for their military execution, so that they rested on the fifteenth day, and made that their thanksgiving-day, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.18">v. 18</reference>. Both of them celebrated their festival the very day after they had finished their work and gained their point. When we have received signal mercies from God we ought to be quick and speedy in making our thankful returns to him, while the mercy is fresh and the impressions of it are most sensible.
entries.a15814ccb9340d70739c09398bf6befe13b60975: <div eID="gen9110" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Feast of Purim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 509.)</title> <div sID="gen9111" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters unto all the Jews that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, <hi type="italic">both</hi> nigh and far, <hi type="super">21</hi> To stablish <hi type="italic">this</hi> among them, that they should keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar, and the fifteenth day of the same, yearly, <hi type="super">22</hi> As the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day: that they should make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordecai had written unto them; <hi type="super">24</hi> Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that <hi type="italic">is,</hi> the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them; <hi type="super">25</hi> But when <hi type="italic">Esther</hi> came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows. <hi type="super">26</hi> Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name of Pur. Therefore for all the words of this letter, and <hi type="italic">of that</hi> which they had seen concerning this matter, and which had come unto them, <hi type="super">27</hi> The Jews ordained, and took upon them, and upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them, so as it should not fail, that they would keep these two days according to their writing, and according to their <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> time every year; <hi type="super">28</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> these days <hi type="italic">should be</hi> remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and <hi type="italic">that</hi> these days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews, nor the memorial of them perish from their seed. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority, to confirm this second letter of Purim. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he sent the letters unto all the Jews, to the hundred twenty and seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, <hi type="italic">with</hi> words of peace and truth, <hi type="super">31</hi> To confirm these days of Purim in their times <hi type="italic">appointed,</hi> according as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined them, and as they had decreed for themselves and for their seed, the matters of the fastings and their cry. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book. <div eID="gen9111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9112" type="x-p"/> We may well imagine how much affected Mordecai and Esther were with the triumphs of the Jews over their enemies, and how they saw the issue of that decisive day with a satisfaction proportionable to the care and concern with which they expected it. How were their hearts enlarged with joy in God and his salvation, and what new songs of praise were put into their mouths! But here we are told what course they took to spread the knowledge of it among their people, and to perpetuate the remembrance of it to posterity, for the honour of God and the encouragement of his people to trust in him at all times. <div eID="gen9112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9113" type="x-p"/> I. The history was written, and copies of it were dispersed among all the Jews in all the provinces of the empire, <hi type="italic">both nigh and far,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.20">v. 20</reference>. They all knew something of the story, being nearly concerned in it—were by the first edict made sensible of their danger and by the second of their deliverance; but how this amazing turn was given they could not tell. Mordecai therefore <hi type="italic">wrote all these things.</hi> And if this book be the same that he wrote, as many think it is, I cannot but observe what a difference there is between Mordecai's style and Nehemiah's. Nehemiah, at every turn, takes notice of divine Providence and the <hi type="italic">good hand of his God</hi> upon him, which is very proper to stir up devout affections in the minds of his readers; but Mordecai never so much as mentions the name of God in the whole story. Nehemiah wrote his book at Jerusalem, where religion was in fashion and an air of it appeared in men's common conversation; Mordecai wrote his at Shushan the palace, where policy reigned more then piety, and he wrote according to the genius of the place. Even those that have the root of the matter in them are apt to lose the savour of religion, and let their leaf wither, when they converse wholly with those that have little religion. Commend me to Nehemiah's way of writing; <hi type="italic">that</hi> I would imitate, and yet learn from Mordecai's that men may be truly devout though they do not abound in the shows and expressions of devotion, and therefore that we must not judge nor despise our brethren. But, because there is so little of the language of Canaan in this book, many think it was not written by Mordecai, but was an extract out of the journals of the kings of Persia, giving an account of the matter of fact, which the Jews themselves knew how to comment upon. <div eID="gen9113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9114" type="x-p"/> II. A festival was instituted, to be observed yearly from generation to generation by the Jews, in remembrance of this wonderful work which God wrought for them, that <hi type="italic">the children who should be born</hi> might know it, and <hi type="italic">declare it to their children, that they might set their hope in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.6-Ps.78.7">Ps. lxxviii. 6, 7</reference>. It would be for the honour of God as the protector of his people, and the honour of Israel as the care of Heaven, a confirmation of the fidelity of God's covenant, an invitation to strangers to come into the bonds of it, and an encouragement to God's own people cheerfully to depend upon his wisdom, power, and goodness, in the greatest straits. Posterity would reap the benefit of this deliverance, and therefore ought to celebrate the memorial of it. Now concerning this festival we are here told, <div eID="gen9114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9115" type="x-p"/> 1. When it was observed—every year on <hi type="italic">the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the twelfth month,</hi> just a month before the passover, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.21">v. 21</reference>. Thus the first month and the last month of the year kept in remembrance the months that were past, even <hi type="italic">the days when God preserved them.</hi> They kept two days together as thanksgiving days, and did not think them too much to spend in praising God. Let us not be niggardly in our returns of praise to him who bestows his favours so liberally upon us. Observe, They did not keep the day when they fought, but the days when they rested, and on the fifteenth those in Shushan, and both those days they kept. The sabbath was appointed not on the day that God finished his work, but on the day that he <hi type="italic">rested from it.</hi> The modern Jews observe the thirteenth day, the day appointed for their destruction, as a fasting-day, grounding the practice on <reference osisRef="Esth.9.31">v. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">the matters of their fastings and cry.</hi> But that refers to what was in the day of their distress (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.3">ch. iv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.16">16</reference>), which was not to be continued when God had turned their fasts into <hi type="italic">joy and gladness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.8.19">Zech. viii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen9115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9116" type="x-p"/> 2. How it was called—<hi type="italic">The feast of Purim</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.26">(v. 26</reference>), from <hi type="italic">Pur,</hi> a Persian word which signified <hi type="italic">a lot,</hi> because Haman had by lot determined this to be the time of the Jews' destruction, but the Lord, at whose disposal the lot is, had determined it to be the time of their triumph. The name of this festival would remind them of the sovereign dominion of the God of Israel, who served his own purposes by the foolish superstitions of the heathen, and outwitted the <hi type="italic">monthly prognosticators</hi> in their own craft (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Isa. xlvii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">frustrating the tokens of the liars and making the diviners mad,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.25-Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 25, 26</reference>. <div eID="gen9116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9117" type="x-p"/> 3. By whom it was instituted and enacted. It was not a divine institution, and therefore it is not called a <hi type="italic">holy day,</hi> but a human appointment, by which it was made a <hi type="italic">good day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">v. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">22</reference>. (1.) The Jews ordained it, and took it upon themselves (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.27">v. 27</reference>), voluntarily <hi type="italic">undertook to do as they had begun.</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.23">v. 23</reference>. They bound themselves to this by common consent. (2.) Mordecai and Esther confirmed their resolve, that it might be the more binding on posterity, and might come well recommended by those great names. They <hi type="italic">wrote,</hi> [1.] <hi type="italic">With all authority</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.29">v. 29</reference>), as well they might, Esther being queen and Mordecai prime-minister of state. It is well when those who are in authority use their authority to authorize that which is good. [2.] <hi type="italic">With words of peace and truth.</hi> Though they wrote with authority, they wrote with tenderness, not imperious, not imposing, but in such language as the council at Jerusalem use in their decree (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.29">Acts xv. 29</reference>): "If you do so and so, <hi type="italic">you shall do well. Fare you well.</hi>" Such was the style of these letters, or such the salutation or valediction of them: <hi type="italic">Peace and truth be with you.</hi> <div eID="gen9117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> 4. By whom it was to be observed—by <hi type="italic">all the Jews,</hi> and by <hi type="italic">their seed,</hi> and by all such as <hi type="italic">joined themselves to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.27">v. 27</reference>. The observance of this feast was to be both universal and perpetual; the proselytes must observe it, in token of their sincere affection to the Jewish nation and their having united interests with them. A concurrence in joys and praises is one branch of the communion of saints. <div eID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> 5. Why it was to be observed—that the memorial of the great things God had done for his church might never <hi type="italic">perish from their seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.28">v. 28</reference>. God does not work wonders for a day, but to be had in everlasting remembrance. <hi type="italic">What he does shall be forever,</hi> and therefore should for ever be had in mind, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. In this affair they would remember, (1.) Haman's bad practices against the church, to his perpetual reproach (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because he had devised against the Jews to destroy them.</hi> Let this be kept in mind, that God's people may never be secure, while they have such malicious enemies, on whom they ought to have a jealous eye. Their enemies aim at no less then their destruction; on God therefore let them depend for salvation. (2.) Esther's good services to the church, to her immortal honour. When Esther, in peril of her life, <hi type="italic">came before the king,</hi> he repealed the edict, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.25">v. 25</reference>. This also must be remembered, that wherever this feast should be kept, and this history read in explication of it, this which she did might be <hi type="italic">told for a memorial of her.</hi> Good deeds done for the Israel of God ought to be remembered, for the encouragement of others to do the like. God will not forget them, and therefore we must not. (3.) Their own prayers, and the answers given to them (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">The matters of their fastings and their cry.</hi> The more cries we have offered up in our trouble, and the more prayers for deliverance, the more we are obliged to be thankful to God for deliverance. <hi type="italic">Call upon me in the time of trouble,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">offer to God thanksgiving.</hi> <div eID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> 6. How it was to be observed. And of this let us see, <div eID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> (1.) What was here enjoined, which was very good, that they should make it, [1.] A day of cheerfulness, <hi type="italic">a day of feasting and joy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">v. 22</reference>), and <hi type="italic">a feast was made for laughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.19">Eccl. x. 19</reference>. When God gives us cause to rejoice why should we not express our joy? [2.] A day of generosity, <hi type="italic">sending portions one to another,</hi> in token of their pleasantness and mutual respect, and their being knit by this and other public common dangers and deliverances so much the closer to each other in love. Friends have their goods in common. [3.] A day of charity, sending <hi type="italic">gifts to the poor.</hi> It is not to our kinsmen and rich neighbours only that we are to send tokens, but to <hi type="italic">the poor and the maimed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.12-Luke.14.13">Luke xiv. 12, 13</reference>. Those that have received mercy must, in token of their gratitude, show mercy; and there never wants occasion, for the poor we have always with us. Thanksgiving and almsgiving should go together, that, when we are rejoicing and blessing God, the heart of the poor may rejoice with us and their loins may bless us. <div eID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was added to this, which was much better. They always, at the feast, read the whole story over in the synagogue each day, and put up three prayers to God, in the first of which they praise God for counting them worthy to attend this divine service; in the second they thank him for the miraculous preservation of their ancestors; in the third they praise him that they have lived to observe another festival in memory of it. So bishop Patrick. <div eID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9123" type="x-p"/> (3.) What it has since degenerated to, which is much worse. Their own writers acknowledge that this feast is commonly celebrated among them with gluttony, and drunkenness, and excess of riot. Their Talmud says expressly that, in the feast of Purim, a man should drink till he knows not the difference between <hi type="italic">Cursed be Haman,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Blessed be Mordecai.</hi> See what the corrupt and wicked nature of man often brings that to which was at first well intended: here is a religious feast turned into a carnival, a perfect revel, as wakes are among us. Nothing more purifies the heart and adorns religion than holy joy; nothing more pollutes the heart and reproaches religion than carnal mirth and sensual pleasure. <hi type="italic">Corruptio optimi est pessima—What is best becomes when corrupted the worst.</hi>  <chapter eID="Esth.9"/> <div eID="gen9123" type="x-p"/>

entries.72f24414823c69890c00ded7c0ba675d7f1ada3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4450"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.9.1-Esth.9.19">Es 9:1-19</reference>. The Jews Slay Their Enemies with the Ten Sons of Haman.</title> <div sID="gen6435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4450"/><hi type="bold">1. in the twelfth month, ... on the thirteenth day of the same--</hi>This was the day which Haman's superstitious advisers had led him to select as the most fortunate for the execution of his exterminating scheme against the Jews [Es 3:7]. <div eID="gen6435" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc90d963d8544c727081614504310656d897e351: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4451"/><div sID="gen6436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4451"/><hi type="bold">2. The Jews gathered themselves ... no man could withstand them--</hi>The tables were now turned in their favor; and though their enemies made their long meditated attack, the Jews were not only at liberty to act on the defensive, but through the powerful influence enlisted on their side at court together with the blessing of God, they were everywhere victorious.<div eID="gen6436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fear of them fell upon all people--</hi>This impression arose not alone from the consciousness of the all-powerful vizier being their countryman, but from the hand of God appearing so visibly interposed to effect their strange and unexpected deliverance. <div eID="gen6437" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c21742e25092a6a014267719d84373f67fcf799: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4452"/><div sID="gen6438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4452"/><hi type="bold">5-16. Thus the Jews smote all their enemies--</hi>The effect of the two antagonistic decrees was, in the meantime, to raise a fierce and bloody war between the Jews and their enemies throughout the Persian empire; but through the dread of Esther and Mordecai, the provincial governors universally favored their cause, so that their enemies fell in great numbers. <div eID="gen6438" type="x-p"/>
entries.83b8ba08e4945a19b22dac170211bccccf3c16f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4454"/><div sID="gen6440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4454"/><hi type="bold">19. a day of ... feasting ... of sending portions one to another--</hi>The princes and people of the East not only invite their friends to feasts, but it is their custom to send a portion of the banquet to those who cannot well come to it, especially their relations, and those who are detained at home in a state of sorrow or distress. <div eID="gen6440" type="x-p"/>
entries.64b4004681b26f281ffd8a601be9f7563a6ae68f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4455"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.9.20-Esth.9.32">Es 9:20-32</reference>. The Two Days of Purim Made Festival.</title> <div sID="gen6441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4455"/><hi type="bold">20. Mordecai wrote these things--</hi>Commentators are not agreed what is particularly meant by "these things"; whether the letters following, or an account of these marvellous events to be preserved in the families of the Jewish people, and transmitted from one generation to another. <div eID="gen6441" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cbbf5828d14365a8fc7b274a9c3cc4a944bc5c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4456"/><div sID="gen6442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4456"/><hi type="bold">26. they called these days Purim after the name of Pur--</hi>"Pur," in the Persian language, signifies "lot"; and the feast of Purim, or lots, has a reference to the time having been pitched upon by Haman through the decision of the lot. In consequence of the signal national deliverance which divine providence gave them from the infamous machinations of Haman, Mordecai ordered the Jews to commemorate that event by an anniversary festival, which was to last for two days, in accordance with the two days' war of defense they had to maintain. There was a slight difference in the time of this festival; for the Jews in the provinces, having defended themselves against their enemies on the thirteenth, devoted the fourteenth to festivity; whereas their brethren in Shushan, having extended that work over two days, did not observe their thanksgiving feast till the fifteenth. But this was remedied by authority, which fixed the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar. It became a season of sunny memories to the universal body of the Jews; and, by the letters of Mordecai, dispersed through all parts of the Persian empire, it was established as an annual feast, the celebration of which is kept up still. On both days of the feast, the modern Jews read over the Megillah or Book of Esther in their synagogues. The copy read must not be printed, but written on vellum in the form of a roll; and the names of the ten sons of Haman are written on it a peculiar manner, being ranged, they say, like so many bodies on a gibbet. The reader must pronounce all these names in one breath. Whenever Haman's name is pronounced, they make a terrible noise in the synagogue. Some drum with their feet on the floor, and the boys have mallets with which they knock and make a noise. They prepare themselves for their carnival by a previous fast, which should continue three days, in imitation of Esther's; but they have mostly reduced it to one day [Jennings, Jewish Antiquities]. <chapter eID="Esth.9"/>

entries.2e4ebe8ff4846d3ab50238f97d4c44e983c4eedc: <div eID="gen15612" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15613" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15614" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15614" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15613" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15615" type="x-p"/> On the thirteenth of the month Adar the Jews destroy their enemies, and the governors of the provinces assist them, <reference osisRef="Est.9.1-Est.9.5">Est 9:1-5</reference>. They slay five hundred in Shushan, and kill the ten sons of Haman, but take no spoil, <reference osisRef="Est.9.6-Est.9.10">Est 9:6-10</reference>. The king is informed of the slaughter in Shushan, <reference osisRef="Est.9.11">Est 9:11</reference>. He desires to know what Esther requests farther; who begs that the Jews may be permitted to act on the following day as they had done on the preceding, and that Haman's sons may be hanged upon the gallows; which is granted; and they slay three hundred more in Shushan, and in the other provinces seventy-five thousand, <reference osisRef="Est.9.12-Est.9.16">Est 9:12-16</reference>. A recapitulation of what was done; and of the appointment of the feast of Purim to be observed through all their generations every year, <reference osisRef="Est.9.17-Est.9.28">Est 9:17-28</reference>. Esther writes to confirm this appointment, <reference osisRef="Est.9.29-Est.9.32">Est 9:29-32</reference>. <div eID="gen15615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15617" type="x-p"/> Now in the twelfth month - What a number of providences, and none of them apparently of an extraordinary nature, concurred to preserve a people so signally, and to all human appearance so inevitably, doomed to destruction! None are ever too low for God to lift up, or too high for God to cast down. Must not these heathens have observed that the uncontrollable hand of an Almighty Being had worked in behalf of the Jews? And must not this have had a powerful tendency to discredit the idolatry of the country?
entries.cab7ad31bd548aac797d5636719b0d180bc551be: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15618" type="x-p"/> And all the rulers of the provinces - Mordecai being raised to the highest confidence of the king, and to have authority over the whole realm, these officers assisted the Jews, no doubt, with the troops under their command, to overthrow those who availed themselves of the former decree to molest the Jews. For it does not appear that the Jews slew any person who did not rise up to destroy them. See <reference osisRef="Est.9.5">Est 9:5</reference>.
entries.22ef41062b5766a16cf25ff4fdfa367b688f66a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15619" type="x-p"/> And in Shushan - It is strange that in this city, where the king's mind must have been so well known, there should be found five hundred persons to rise up in hostility against those whom they knew the king befriended!
entries.3b4a5fcfb6fa13732f47fd13f39c508fd4ec4a04: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15620" type="x-p"/> The ten sons of Haman - Their names are given above. And it is remarked here, and in <reference osisRef="Est.9.16">Est 9:16</reference>, where the account is given of the number slain in the provinces, that the Jews laid no hands on the spoil. They stood for their lives, and gave full proof that they sought their own personal safety, and not the property of their enemies, though the decree in their favor gave them authority to take the property of all those who were their adversaries, <reference osisRef="Est.8.11">Est 8:11</reference>.
entries.7cee89517739656661b2bca5503a8293a802b010: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15621" type="x-p"/> Let Haman's ten sons be hanged - They had been slain the preceding day, and now she requests that they may be exposed on posts or gibbets, as a terror to those who sought the destruction of the Jews.
entries.c0bc8c96932f06bd6ac0908de5f66925f41b95e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15622" type="x-p"/> And slew three hundred men - Esther had probably been informed by Mordecai that there were still many enemies of the Jews who sought their destruction, who had escaped the preceding day; and, therefore, begs that this second day be added to the former permission. This being accordingly granted, they found three hundred more, in all eight hundred. And thus Susa was purged of all their enemies.
entries.2999ae191c5466d40eea6f9aa98135ef36edf84d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen15622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15623" type="x-p"/> The Jews - assembled - on the thirteenth - and on the fourteenth - These two days they were employed in slaying their enemies; and they rested on the fifteenth.
entries.4ade0dbff959f8d95352df5cb93b81b80abb4223: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15624" type="x-p"/> The Jews of the villages - They joined that to the preceding day, and made it a day of festivity, and of sending portions to each other; that is, the rich sent portions of the sacrifices slain on this occasion to the poor, that they also might be enabled to make the day a day of festivity; that as the sorrow was general, so also might the joy be. <div eID="gen15624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15625" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark that the ancient Itala or Ante-hieronymian version of this book omits the whole of these nineteen verses. Query, Were they originally in this book?
entries.c1ca4a1e32f5dc04e70bd5f5777c6c86efc534e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen15625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15626" type="x-p"/> Mordecai wrote these things - It has been supposed that thus far that part of the book of Esther, which was written by Mordecai extends: what follows to the end, was probably added either by Ezra, or the men of the Great Synagogue; though what is said here may refer only to the letters sent by Mordecai to the Jews of the provinces. From this to the end of the chapter is nothing else than a recapitulation of the chief heads of the preceding history, and an account of the appointment of an annual feast, called the feast of Purim, in commemoration of their providential deliverance from the malice of Haman.
entries.bbe35ece552a0087d1835ea55eddd5ae5a904dcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen15626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15627" type="x-p"/> The Jews undertook to do as they had begun - They had already kept the fifteenth day, and some of them in the country the fourteenth also, as a day of rejoicing: Mordecai wrote to them to bind themselves and their successors, and all their proselytes, to celebrate this as an annual feast throughout all their generations; and this they undertook to do. And it has been observed among them, in all places of their dispersion, from that day to the present time, without any interruption.
entries.148f0aeee1cb93847bac7e15ee721d2757574208: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen15627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15628" type="x-p"/> They called these days Purim - That is from pari, the lot; because, as we have seen, Haman cast lots to find what month, and what day of the month, would be the most favorable for the accomplishment of his bloody designs against the Jews. See on <reference osisRef="Est.3.7">Est 3:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen15628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15629" type="x-p"/> And of that which they had seen - The first letter to which this second refers, must be that sent by Mordecai himself. See <reference osisRef="Est.9.20">Est 9:20</reference>.
entries.03b777bc673f310fa837a65025faf2054aa38414: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen15629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15630" type="x-p"/> Esther - wrote with all authority - Esther and Mordecai had the king's license so to do: and their own authority was great and extensive.
entries.d6662e833b86a54d9f8223ddaf8c6c66351fa0a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen15630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15631" type="x-p"/> As they had decreed for themselves and for their seed - There is no mention of their receiving the approbation of any high priest, nor of any authority beyond that of Mordecai and Esther; the king could not join in such a business, as he had nothing to do with the Jewish religion, that not being the religion of the country.
entries.9d556b16a99e10102e2abc6ee694a2624bd0813f: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen15631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15632" type="x-p"/> The decree of Esther confirmed these matters - It was received by the Jews universally with all respect, and they bound themselves to abide by it. <div eID="gen15632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15633" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate gives a strange turn to this verse: Et omnia quae libri hujus, qui vocatur Esther, historia continentur; "And all things which are contained in the history of this book, which is called Esther." <div eID="gen15633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15634" type="x-p"/> The Targum says, And by the word of Esther all these things relative to Purim were confirmed; and the roll was transcribed in this book. The Syriac is the same as the Hebrew, and the Septuagint in this place not very different.  <chapter eID="Esth.9"/> <div eID="gen15634" type="x-p"/>

entries.32a154646f67e7e7c98b2542c5f28abfcf07dda7: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.1">Est 9:1</reference> <hi type="italic">The Jews avenged of their enemies.</hi> - Est 9:1. In the twelfth month, on the thirteenth day of the same - the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities, etc. Several parenthetical clauses succeed this definition of time, so that the statement of what then took place does not follow till נקהלוּ, Est 9:2. These parenthetical clauses state not only the meaning of the day just named, but also give a general notice of the conflict between the Jews and their enemies. The first runs: “when the word of the king drew nigh and his decree to be done,” i.e., when the execution of the royal decree approached. The second is: “on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have the mastery of them, and it was changed (i.e., the contrary occurred), that the Jews had the mastery over them that hated them.” בּ שׁלט, to rule, to have the mastery over. נהפוך is <hi type="italic">infin. abs.,</hi> used instead of the <hi type="italic">imperf</hi>. הוּא is referred by Bertheau to יום: the day was changed from a day of misfortune to a day of prosperity for the Jews, alluding to <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">Est 9:22</reference>; but it is not a change of the day which is here spoken of, but a change of the hope of the enemies into its opposite; hence we must regard הוּא as neuter: it was changed, i.e., the contrary occurred. The pronoun המּה serves to emphasize the subject; comp. Ewald, §314, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, who in this and similar cases takes הוּא המּה in the sense of <hi type="italic">ipse, ipsi</hi>.
entries.27f44810d79e36c2886a3a28be9fa58b85b77cc6: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.2-Esth.9.3">Est 9:2-3</reference> בּעריהם, in their cities, i.e., the cities in which they dwelt in all the dominions of the king. יד לשׁלח, to stretch out the hand (as also in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Est 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.3.6">Est 3:6</reference>, for the purpose of killing) against those who sought their hurt, i.e., sought to destroy them. “And no one stood before them (בּפני עמד, like <reference osisRef="Josh.10.8">Jos 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.42">Jos 21:42</reference>, and elsewhere), because the fear of them fell upon all people (see rem. on <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Est 8:17</reference>). And all the rulers of the provinces, and the satraps and governors (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.8.9">Est 8:9</reference>), and those that did the king’s business (המּלאכה עשׁי, see rem. on <reference osisRef="Esth.3.9">Est 3:9</reference>), supported the Jews (נשּׂא like Ezr 1:4), because the fear of Mordochai fell upon them.”
entries.1f80f7fd1bfe5b46bd0cdbda26e40e9262a1e376: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.4">Est 9:4</reference> “For Mordochai was great in the king’s house (was much esteemed by the king), and his fame went through all the provinces (שׁמעו as in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.27">Jos 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.9.9">Jos 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">Jer 6:24</reference>); for this man Mordochai became continually greater;” comp. <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12">2Ch 17:12</reference>, where the partic. גּדל stands instead of the inf. abs. גּדול.
entries.0060d393e6e995555f30818c9a2024521a1577ad: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.5">Est 9:5</reference> <div eID="gen6796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6797" type="x-p"/> Thus supported, the Jews inflicted defeat upon their enemies with the sword, and with slaughter and destruction. הכּה with בּ, to deal a blow upon or against some one, to cause or bring about upon enemies a defeat; comp. e.g., <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.10">2Sa 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.17">2Sa 24:17</reference>; Num 22:6. The notion is strengthened by וגו מכּת־חרב, literally, to strike a stroke of the sword, and of slaughter, and of destruction, in accordance with the decree, Est 8:11. “And did according to their will to those that hated them,” i.e., retaliated upon their enemies at their discretion.
entries.38e4ea552a36084c7a5ec131510c135b983cee38: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.6">Est 9:6</reference> <div eID="gen6797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6798" type="x-p"/> In the citadel of Susa they destroyed (in round numbers) 500 men.
entries.3aa9b51a2b1aa8140a7b94a9c254a6761a5f59c0: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.7-Esth.9.10">Est 9:7-10</reference> <div eID="gen6798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6799" type="x-p"/> Also they slew the ten sons of Haman, whose names are given, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.7-Esth.9.9">Est 9:7-9</reference>;<note placement="foot">The peculiar position of the names of the sons of Haman in editions of the Bible, grounded as it is upon the ancient mode of writing, must originally have been intended merely to give prominence to the names, and facilitate their computation. The later Rabbis, however, have endeavoured to discover therein some deeper meaning. This mode of writing the names has been said to be <hi type="italic">signum voti, ut a ruina sua nunquam amplius resurgant,</hi> or also a sign <hi type="italic">quod sicut hi decem filii in linea perpendiculari, unus supra alterum, suspensi fuerint</hi>. Comp. Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Synagoga jud</hi>. pp. 157-159 of the Basle edit. 1580. What is indicated by the smaller forms of the letters ת, שׁ, and ז, in the first, seventh, and tenth names, is not known; the larger ו in the tenth may have been meant to give prominence, by the character employed, to this name as the last.</note> but on the spoil they laid not their hand, though this was allowed to them, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">Est 8:11</reference>, as it had been commanded to their enemies by Haman’s edict, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.13">Est 3:13</reference>, <hi type="italic">ut ostenderent, se non aliud quam vitae suae incolumitatem quaerere; hanc enim perdere volebant ii qui occidebantur.</hi> C. a Lapide.
entries.f565eef5fed8c7c728c3aead8da688fdb8b36fe8: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.11-Esth.9.12">Est 9:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen6799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6800" type="x-p"/> When on the same day an account was given to the king of the result of the conflict, and the number of those slain in Susa reported, he announced to Queen Esther: the Jews have slain in the citadel of Susa 500 men and the ten sons of Haman; “what have they done in the rest of the king’s provinces?” i.e., if they have killed 500 men in Susa, how many may they not have slain in other parts of the kingdom? and then asked her what else she wished or required. With respect to the words, comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.5.6">Est 5:6</reference>, and Est 7:2.
entries.c3e8c2329856108f28511476b971b69566b063c0: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.13">Est 9:13</reference> <div eID="gen6800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6801" type="x-p"/> Esther requested: “let it be granted to the Jews which are in Susa to do to-morrow also according to the decree of to-day (i.e., exactly as to-day), and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged upon the tree,” i.e., their dead bodies nailed on crosses - <hi type="italic">majoris infamiae causa,</hi> according to Hebrew and Persian custom; comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.21.22">Deu 21:22</reference> and the explanation of Ezr 6:11. On the motive for this request, see above, p. 194.
entries.cbb609756048b2a0b0656f64750014684c6a2e23: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.14">Est 9:14</reference> <div eID="gen6801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6802" type="x-p"/> The king commanded it so to be done. “Then was a decree given at Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.” The decree given in Susa does not refer to the hanging of the sons of Haman, but to the permission given to the Jews to fight against their enemies on the morrow also. This is required not only by a comparison of <reference osisRef="Esth.8.13">Est 8:13</reference>, but also by the connection of the present verse; for in consequence of this decree the Jews assembled on the 14th Adar (comp. ויּקּהלוּ, then they assembled themselves, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.15">Est 9:15</reference>), while the hanging of the sons of Haman, on the contrary, is related in an accessory clause by a simple perfect, תּלוּ.
entries.276b3e5ef80414acda284058e6b43d9f397106d5: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.15-Esth.9.17">Est 9:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen6802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6803" type="x-p"/> On this second day the Jews slew 300 more; comp. Est 9:10. - Est 9:16. The rest of the Jews in the provinces, i.e., the Jews in the other parts of the kingdom, assembled themselves and stood for their lives, and had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes 75,000, but upon the spoil they laid not their hand. על עמד like Est 8:11. The מאיביהם ונוח inserted between על נ ועמד and והרוג is striking; we should rather have expected the resting or having rest from their enemies after the death of the latter, as in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.17">Est 9:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.9.18">Est 9:18</reference>, where this is plainly stated to have taken place on the day after the slaughter. The position of these words is only explained by the consideration, that the narrator desired at once to point out how the matter ended. The narrative continues in the <hi type="italic">infin. abs.</hi> instead of expressing this clause by the <hi type="italic">infin. constr.,</hi> and so causing it to be governed by what precedes. Thus - as Ew. §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, remarks - all the possible hues of the sentence fade into this grey and formless termination (viz., the use of the <hi type="italic">infin. absol.</hi> instead of the <hi type="italic">verb. fin.</hi>). This inaccuracy of diction does not justify us, however, in assuming that we have here an interpolation or an alteration in the text. The statement of the day is given in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.17">Est 9:17</reference>, and then the clause following is again added in the <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi>: “and they rested on the 14th day of the same (of Adar), and made it a day of feasting and gladness.”
entries.5386c2b703b7559bb488dcc06e25b38310f48bba: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.18-Esth.9.19">Est 9:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen6803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6804" type="x-p"/> The Jews in Susa, on the other hand, who were both on the 13th and 14th Adar still fighting against their enemies, and did not rest till the 15th, made this latter their day of rejoicing. - In <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Est 9:19</reference> it is again stated that the Jews in the country towns and villages made the 14th their day of gladness, and this statement is appended by על־כּן to make this appear the result of what precedes. The <hi type="italic">Chethiv</hi> הפּרוזים is perhaps an Aramaic expression for פּרזים, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference> and 1Sa 6:18. פּרוזי means the inhabitants of the open, i.e., unfortified, towns and villages of the plains in contrast to the fortified capital; see on Deu 3:5. On פּרזות, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.11">Eze 38:11</reference>; Zec 2:8. וגו מנות משׁלוח, and of mutual sending of gifts, i.e., portions of food; comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh 8:10</reference>, Neh 8:12.
entries.d03201b734c066c1a343d6ed424b09bbc0f7dfc7: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.20-Esth.9.22">Est 9:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen6804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> The feast of Purim instituted by letters from Mordochai and Esther. Est 9:20. Mordochai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews, etc. האלּה הדּברים does not mean the contents of the present book but the events of the last days, especially the fact that the Jews, after overcoming their enemies, rested in Susa on the 15th, in the other provinces on the 14th Adar, and kept these days as days of rejoicing. This is obvious from the object of these letters, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.21">Est 9:21</reference> : וגו עליהם לקיּם, to appoint among them “that they should keep the 14th day of the month Adar and the 15th day of the same yearly, as the days on which the Jews rested from their enemies, and as the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a glad day, that they should keep them as days of feasting and joy, and of mutual sending of portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.” יום עשׂה, to keep, to celebrate a day. The עשׂים להיות, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.21">Est 9:21</reference>, is after long parentheses taken up again in אותם לעשׂות. קיּם, to establish a matter, to authorize it, comp. Rth 4:7. Both the 14th and 15th Adar were made festivals because the Jews on them had rest from their enemies, and celebrated this rest by feasting, some on the former, some on the latter day.
entries.6cbab03901d8c7537a0832a95cd9fb36e885cc7d: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.23">Est 9:23</reference> <div eID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordochai had written to them. They had begun, as <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">Est 9:22</reference> tells us, by keeping both days, and Mordochai wrote to them that they should make this an annual custom. This they agreed to do in consequence of Mordochai’s letters. The reason of their so doing is given in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.24">Est 9:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.9.25">Est 9:25</reference>, and the name of this festival is explained, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.26">Est 9:26</reference>, by a brief recapitulation of the events which gave rise to it. Then follows, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Esth.9.26">Est 9:26</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Esth.9.27">Est 9:27</reference>, another wordy statement of the fact, that it was by reason of this letter, and on account of what they had seen, i.e., experienced, that the annual celebration of this feast was instituted for a perpetual memorial to all Jews at all times (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.28">Est 9:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.9.29">Est 9:29</reference>).
entries.78cfc2580ca8dfa5447a5f4ed1abdd9aa54e7c8a: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.24">Est 9:24</reference> <div eID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6807" type="x-p"/> For Haman, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.3.1">Est 3:1</reference>, Est 3:6.), and had cast Pur, that is the lot (see on <reference osisRef="Esth.3.7">Est 3:7</reference>), to consume them and to destroy them. המם, mostly used of the discomfiture with which God destroys the enemies, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.15">Deu 2:15</reference>, and elsewhere.
entries.7fb7e2bdf3c8d919bf595e72d7faf4a26aa8f6a4: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.25">Est 9:25</reference> וּבבאהּ, and when it (the matter), not when she, Esther, came before the king, - for Esther is not named in the context, - he commanded by letters (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.8">Est 8:8</reference>), i.e., he gave the written order: let the wicked device which he devised against the Jews return upon his own head; and they hanged him and his sons upon the tree.
entries.41d0c311fc760c89e1207dbce20e18a22f3d2929: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.26-Esth.9.27">Est 9:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen6807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6808" type="x-p"/> Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name Pur. This first על־כּן refers to what precedes and states the reason, resulting from what has just been mentioned, why this festival received the name of <hi type="italic">Purim</hi>. With the second על־כּן begins a new sentence which reaches to <reference osisRef="Esth.9.28">Est 9:28</reference>, and explains how it happened that these feast-days became a general observance with all Jews; namely, that because of all the words of this letter (of Mordochai, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.20">Est 9:20</reference>), and of what they had seen concerning the matter (על־כּכה, concerning so and so), and what had come upon them (therefore for two reasons: (1) because of the written injunction of Mordochai; and (2) because they had themselves experienced this event), the Jews established, and took upon themselves, their descendants, and all who should join themselves unto them (proselytes), so that it should not fail (i.e., inviolably), to keep (to celebrate) these two days according to the writing concerning them and the time appointed thereby year by year.
entries.64bd867c55da22f7f60e008dfc44fc35e645d549: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.28">Est 9:28</reference> <div eID="gen6808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6809" type="x-p"/> And that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and these days of Purim are not to pass away among the Jews, nor their remembrance to cease among their seed. The participles ונעשׂים נזכּרים still depend on להיות, Est 9:27. Not till the last clause does the construction change in להיות לא to the <hi type="italic">temp. finit.</hi> יעבור ולא is a periphrasis of the adverb: imperishably, inviolably. כּכתבם, <hi type="italic">secundum scriptum eorum,</hi> i.e., as Mordochai had written concerning them (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.23">Est 9:23</reference>). כּזמנּם, as he had appointed their time. מן סוּף, to come to an end from, i.e., to cease among their descendants.
entries.abb0dc2b115514e1519a062b10b62d69a2a1f3cd: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.29">Est 9:29</reference> <div eID="gen6809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6810" type="x-p"/> A second letter from Queen Esther and Mordochai to appoint fasting and lamentation on the days of Purim. Est 9:29. And Esther the queen and Mordochai the Jew wrote with all strength, that is very forcibly, to appoint this second letter concerning Purim, i.e., to give to the contents of this second letter the force of law. הזּאת refers to what follows, in which the contents of the letter are briefly intimated. The letter is called השּׁנית with reference to the first letter sent by Mordochai, Est 9:20.
entries.633065c7424e370aa625afe143af0cc30d9f5399: <reference osisRef="Esth.9.30-Esth.9.32">Est 9:30-32</reference> <div eID="gen6810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6811" type="x-p"/> And he (Mordochai) sent letters, i.e., copies of the writing mentioned <reference osisRef="Esth.9.29">Est 9:29</reference>, to all the Jews in the 127 provinces (which formed) the kingdom of Ahashverosh, words of peace and truth, i.e., letters containing words of peace and truth (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.31">Est 9:31</reference>), to appoint these days of Purim in their portions of time according as Mordochai the Jew and Esther the queen had appointed, and as they (the Jews) had appointed for themselves and for their descendants, the things (or words = precepts) of the fastings and their lamentations. בּזמנּיהם, in their appointed times; as the suffix relates to the days of Purim, the זמנּים can mean only portions of time in these days. The sense of <reference osisRef="Esth.9.29-Esth.9.31">Est 9:29-31</reference> is as follows: According to the injunctions of Esther and Mordochai, the Jews appointed for themselves and their descendants times also of fasting and lamentation in the days of Purim. To make this appointment binding upon all the Jews in all provinces of the Persian monarchy, Esther and Mordochai published a second letter, which was sent by Mordochai throughout the whole realm of King Ahashverosh. To this is added, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.32">Est 9:32</reference>, that the decree of Esther appointed these matters of Purim, i.e., the injunction mentioned vv. 29-31, also to fast and weep during these days, and it was written in the book. הסּפר, the book in which this decree was written, cannot mean the writing of Esther mentioned. <reference osisRef="Esth.9.29">Est 9:29</reference>, but some written document concerning Purim which has not come down to us, though used as an authority by the author of the present book. The times when the fasting and lamentation were to take place in the days of Purim, are not stated in this verse; this could, however, only be on the day which Haman had appointed for the extermination of the Jews, viz., the 13th Adar. This day is kept by the Jews as אסתּר תּענית, Esther’s fast.<note placement="foot">According to 2 Macc. 15:36, the victory over Nicanor was to be celebrated on the 13th Adar, but, according to a note of Dr. Cassel in Grimm’s <hi type="italic">kurzgef. exeget. Handb. zu den Apokryphen</hi>, on 2 Macc. 15:36, the festival of Nicanor is mentioned in Jewish writings, as Megillat Taanit, c. 12, in the Babylonian Talmud, <hi type="italic">tr. Taanit</hi>, f. 18b, in <hi type="italic">Massechet Sofrim</hi> 17, 4, but has been by no means observed for at least the last thousand years. The book Scheiltot of R. Acha (in the 9th century) speaks of the 13th Adar as a fast-day in memory of the fast of Esther, while even at the time of the Talmud the “Fast of Esther” is spoken of as a three days fast, kept, however, after the feast of Purim. From all this it is obvious, that a diversity of opinions prevailed among the Rabbis concerning the time of this fast of Esther.</note>  <chapter eID="Esth.9"/> <div eID="gen6811" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw in the twelfth month (that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the month Adar) on the thirteenth day of the same, when the kings commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In that day which was selected by <ns0:hi>Haman</ns0:hi> with great Industry and Art, as the most lucky day, and which their Enemies had oft times formerly thought of, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>o doubt threatned the Jews with it.</ns0:note>, (though it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over them that hated them.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities, throughout all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, to lay hand on such as sought their hurt; and no man could withstand them <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Their Enemies though they did and were allowed to take up Arms against them, yet were easily conquered and destroyed by the Jews.</ns0:note>: for the fear of them <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Who had such potent Friends at Court, and so great a God on their side, who by such unusual and prodigious Methods (whereof doubtless they had been particularly informed) had brought about such a mighty and unexpected deliverance.</ns0:note> fell upon all people.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants and the deputies, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>those which did the business that</ns0:hi> belonged <ns0:hi>to the king.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> officers of the king <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> all <ns0:hi>them that did the Kings business; i. e.</ns0:hi> Not only the chief persons designed by the foregoing words, but all his other Ministers or Officers of what quality soever.</ns0:note>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The greatest in Place, and Power, and Favour with the King, both for his near relation to his beloved Queen, and for his good service done to him in preserving his Life, and managing his Affairs; and for those excellent Abilities and Virtues which he dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />covered in him; and especially by the disposition of the heart<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruling God.</ns0:note> in the kings house, and his fame went out throughout all the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vinces: for this man Mordecai waxed greater and greater.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Thus the Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction, and did <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the City so called, as was noted before <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 2. it not being probable either that they would make such a slaughter in the Kings palace, or that they would be suffered so to do.</ns0:note> the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whom by long experience they knew to be their constant and inveterate Enemies, and such as would watch all opportunities to destroy them; which also they might possibly now attempt to do. Part of them also might be Friends and Allies of <ns0:hi>Haman,</ns0:hi> and therefore the avowed Enemies of <ns0:hi>Mordecai.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="11">11 On that day the number of those that were slain in Shushan the palace, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
